newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists to discuss premier on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists to discuss premier on Tuesday.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists said on Monday they had discussed Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev as a possible successor to Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.
The executive bureau is expected to choose a candidate at its regular session on Tuesday. Parvanov said it had decided not to hold the expected leadership plenum.

"The Socialist Party's executive bureau discussed several candidatures at a meeting today and among them is that of Nikolai Dobrev who has agreed to hold the post," party leader Georgi Parvanov told reporters.
"I expect that a new government of the democratic left could be formed even before the prevously announced date of January 16."
The new government -- Bulgaria's ninth since the end of one-party rule in 1989 -- must be approved by parliament, where the Socialists have a majority.

Dobrev, 49, emerged as an outspoken critic of Videnov at last month's party congress where he attacked the cabinet's record in handling the country's economic and social crisis and raised the previously taboo issue of government corruption.
A mining engineer by training, Dobrev was a leader of the Communist youth organisation Komsomol before 1989. He has also chaired parliament's national security committee.
Critics of his candidature say he lacks the economic background necessary to win the approval of Bulgaria's foreign partners.
Parvanov declined to name the other candidates discussed by the party leadership. Parliamentary speaker Blagovest Sendov has also been mentioned as a possible premier.

He said that once the premier is named, the Socialists will hold consultations on a new cabinet with president-elect Petar Stoyanov and with foreign ambassadors to Sofia, mostly from European Union countries.
"We are not indifferent to what they think about the policy of Bulgaria's Democratic Left and its candidature for a prime minister," Parvanov said.
One of the new government's first tasks will be to negotiate implementation of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.
It might also withdraw the 1997 budget bill approved by the outgoing cabinet last week and propose a new one.
